questions.question: Which statement best defines quantization in the context of neural network compression?
questions.choice_A: Mapping high-precision real-valued parameters or activations to a finite set of discrete levels, typically integers, using a prescribed scaling and rounding rule
questions.choice_B: Replacing convolutional layers with fully connected layers to reduce parameter count
questions.choice_C: Pruning weights with small magnitude to create sparse networks
questions.choice_D: Applying dropout to reduce overfitting during training

questions.question: What is dequantization during inference?
questions.choice_A: Computing gradients of quantized parameters to update them
questions.choice_B: Recovering approximate real-valued tensors from stored integers using the inverse of the quantization transform (e.g., scale and zero-point)
questions.choice_C: Rearranging tensor dimensions to improve cache locality
questions.choice_D: Replacing integer arithmetic with floating-point operations for numerical stability

questions.question: In uniform (linear) quantization, which property is true of the quantization decision thresholds?
questions.choice_A: They cluster more densely where the probability density is highest
questions.choice_B: They are chosen by minimizing Kullback–Leibler divergence to a target distribution
questions.choice_C: They are equally spaced along the input range after applying a single global scale (and optional offset)
questions.choice_D: They are learned jointly with model weights during standard training

questions.question: Which is an example of non-uniform quantization relevant to LLM weight compression?
questions.choice_A: Per-tensor symmetric 8-bit linear quantization
questions.choice_B: Saturating arithmetic with max-abs scaling
questions.choice_C: Stochastic rounding with nearest-even tie-breaking
questions.choice_D: k-means codebook quantization where each weight maps to one of K learned centroids

questions.question: Per-tensor, per-channel, and block-wise quantization differ primarily in what aspect?
questions.choice_A: The granularity at which scale (and zero-point) parameters are applied to subsets of a tensor
questions.choice_B: The bit-width used for different parts of the model
questions.choice_C: The activation functions allowed in the quantized model
questions.choice_D: Whether quantization is dynamic or static

questions.question: Why is per-channel (e.g., per-output-channel for convolutions or per-row for linear layers) quantization often preferred over per-tensor for weights?
questions.choice_A: It allows using fewer bits per channel without accuracy loss
questions.choice_B: It reduces quantization error by adapting scale to the dynamic range of each channel, mitigating outlier dominance
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for dequantization entirely
questions.choice_D: It guarantees zero bias in the quantization error

questions.question: What does absolute-max (min–max) scaling compute for symmetric uniform quantization of weights?
questions.choice_A: Scale as the mean absolute deviation divided by the number of quantization levels
questions.choice_B: Scale as the standard deviation times a learned factor
questions.choice_C: Scale as $s = \dfrac{\max(|x|)}{2^{b-1}-1}$ so that the largest magnitude maps to the extreme integer code
questions.choice_D: Scale as $s = \dfrac{\max(x)-\min(x)}{2^b}$ to ensure midrise quantization

questions.question: Which statement about zero-point in asymmetric uniform quantization is correct?
questions.choice_A: Zero-point is unnecessary when the distribution is symmetric
questions.choice_B: Zero-point is the rounding rule used to map values to integers
questions.choice_C: Zero-point increases the number of quantization levels beyond $2^b$
questions.choice_D: Zero-point shifts the integer codebook so that real zero maps exactly to an integer, reducing bias for non-symmetric ranges

questions.question: What is a practical downside of absolute min–max scaling for activations in post-training quantization?
questions.choice_A: It requires labeled data during calibration
questions.choice_B: It cannot be implemented efficiently on GPUs
questions.choice_C: It may be dominated by rare outliers, causing most values to be represented with too few effective levels (excessive clipping or underutilization)
questions.choice_D: It forces the use of symmetric quantization

questions.question: How do percentile/quantile-based calibration methods address outliers?
questions.choice_A: By increasing bit-width where outliers are detected
questions.choice_B: By selecting thresholds based on a high quantile (e.g., 99.9%) of the activation magnitude, intentionally ignoring extreme tails
questions.choice_C: By learning a separate codebook for outliers only
questions.choice_D: By applying log-domain quantization to compress large values

questions.question: Which workflow correctly describes quantized inference for LLM weights stored in int8?
questions.choice_A: Store int8 weights; during inference, dequantize once to float32 at model load and keep using float32 thereafter
questions.choice_B: Store float32 weights; quantize on-the-fly for every matmul to save memory bandwidth
questions.choice_C: Store int8 weights and per-block scales; during each matmul, dequantize tiles into higher precision accumulators, compute, and optionally requantize outputs
questions.choice_D: Store int8 weights and never dequantize; all computations remain in int8 including accumulation

questions.question: In block-wise quantization for LLMs, why are block sizes like 32 or 64 commonly used?
questions.choice_A: They minimize total quantization error globally for any distribution
questions.choice_B: They align with vectorized compute (e.g., tensor cores) and allow local scales that better match variations across weight sub-vectors
questions.choice_C: They avoid the need for storing scale factors entirely
questions.choice_D: They ensure that dequantization can be done without memory accesses

questions.question: Which rounding scheme is often preferred to reduce systematic bias in uniform quantization?
questions.choice_A: Round-to-nearest with stochastic tie-breaking or stochastic rounding, which makes the quantization error approximately zero-mean under mild assumptions
questions.choice_B: Ceiling (round up) because it never underestimates magnitudes
questions.choice_C: Floor (round down) because it preserves sparsity
questions.choice_D: Round toward zero because it reduces overflow

questions.question: What is the typical dequantization formula for asymmetric uniform quantization with scale $s$ and zero-point $z$?
questions.choice_A: $\hat{x} = s\,q$
questions.choice_C: $\hat{x} = q/s + z$
questions.choice_D: $\hat{x} = (q + z)/s$

questions.question: Which trade-off is most accurate when choosing per-tensor vs per-channel scaling for weights?
questions.choice_A: Per-channel reduces memory for scales but increases error
questions.choice_B: Per-tensor reduces error but increases compute
questions.choice_C: Per-channel typically lowers error by adapting to each channel’s range at the cost of storing more scale metadata and potentially more dequant operations
questions.choice_D: There is no trade-off; both are equivalent in practice

questions.question: In histogram-based calibration for activation quantization, what objective is commonly used to select clipping thresholds?
questions.choice_A: Maximize signal-to-noise ratio under $L_\infty$ error
questions.choice_B: Minimize total variation distance between original and quantized histograms
questions.choice_C: Minimize mean absolute error between individual samples
questions.choice_D: Minimize Kullback–Leibler divergence between the original activation distribution and its quantized approximation

questions.question: Why can non-uniform quantization (e.g., logarithmic or learned codebooks) be advantageous for skewed weight distributions?
questions.choice_A: It increases the number of representable values without increasing bit-width
questions.choice_B: It places more code points where the density is high and fewer where it is low, reducing average distortion for a fixed bit budget
questions.choice_C: It eliminates the need for calibration data
questions.choice_D: It guarantees exact recovery after dequantization

questions.question: Which statement best describes quantization bias and how to mitigate it?
questions.choice_A: Bias is the variance of the quantization error; using more bits increases bias
questions.choice_B: Bias is the systematic nonzero mean of the quantization error; symmetric ranges, zero-point calibration, and stochastic rounding can reduce it
questions.choice_C: Bias is the probability of overflow; clipping reduces bias by increasing range
questions.choice_D: Bias occurs only in non-uniform quantization and cannot be mitigated

questions.question: For symmetric uniform quantization of a tensor with range $[-a,a]$ into $b$ bits (signed), which scale is typically used and why?
questions.choice_A: $s = a/2^b$ to align zero with an integer code
questions.choice_B: $s = 2a/(2^b-1)$ so that the endpoints map to the extreme integer codes and the grid is symmetric
questions.choice_C: $s = a/(2^{b-1}-1)$ so that $\pm a$ map to $\pm(2^{b-1}-1)$ in two’s-complement signed integers
questions.choice_D: $s = (a-(-a))/2^b$ to implement midrise quantization with an extra level at zero

questions.question: In practical LLM weight-only post-training quantization (e.g., 8-bit), which statement is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Quantizing only weights typically preserves accuracy well, while activation quantization often requires careful calibration or quantization-aware fine-tuning
questions.choice_B: Activation quantization is always easier than weight quantization because activations are more stationary
questions.choice_C: Per-tensor scales are universally sufficient for Transformer layers
questions.choice_D: Dequantization must always produce float32 values to avoid loss

questions.question: Which is a key practical rationale for block-wise quantization in LLM matmuls over pure per-tensor scaling?
questions.choice_A: Blocks eliminate the need for scale storage and broadcasting
questions.choice_B: Blocks allow fusing dequantize–matmul kernels, improving bandwidth utilization by loading a small scale per block and keeping accumulations in higher precision
questions.choice_C: Blocks ensure exact preservation of layer norms
questions.choice_D: Blocks make zero-point calibration unnecessary
